result: Behavioral data showed that participants exhibited faster reaction times (RTs) when distractors appeared at the high-probability distractor location (HPDL, 848 ms) compared to neutral locations (NL-near: 871 ms, NL-far: 870 ms), demonstrating spatially specific behavioral facilitation due to implicit statistical learning of distractor regularities.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirmed these behavioral findings. Reviewer 1 noted the study provides 'compelling evidence' for distractor suppression effects. Reviewer 2 stated 'the results showed that activity in EVC was suppressed for the location of the salient distractor' and acknowledged the behavioral facilitation. Reviewer 3 praised the 'well-designed' experiment. No concerns were raised about the behavioral RT data or its interpretation.

result: fMRI data revealed that neural populations in early visual cortex (EVC) with receptive fields corresponding to the HPDL showed significantly reduced BOLD responses compared to the far neutral location. Surprisingly, this suppression was spatially broad, extending to nearby neutral locations (NL-near), and occurred regardless of stimulus type (distractor, target, or neutral), indicating stimulus-unspecific suppression that was broader than the spatially specific behavioral effects.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly endorsed these core neural findings. Reviewer 1 stated the study provides 'compelling evidence that activity in the early visual cortex is suppressed at locations that are frequently occupied by a task-irrelevant but salient item' and noted 'this suppression appears to be general to any kind of stimulus.' Reviewer 2 confirmed 'activity in EVC was suppressed for the location of the salient distractor as well as for neighbouring neutral locations' and that 'this suppression was not stimulus specific.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged the findings show 'activity in visual cortex that selectively responds to that location was generally suppressed, in response to all stimuli.'

result: The neural suppression in EVC was spatially specific to receptive fields but extended to nearby neutral locations, occurred regardless of whether distractors, targets, or neutral stimuli were presented, and was stimulus-unspecific, suggesting suppression arises before stimulus identification.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirmed the stimulus-unspecific nature of suppression. Reviewer 1 explicitly stated suppression 'appears to be general to any kind of stimulus.' Reviewer 2 noted 'this suppression was not stimulus specific - meaning it occurred equally for distractors, targets and neutral items.' Reviewer 3 confirmed suppression occurred 'in response to all stimuli (search targets, salient distractors, or neutral items).' No concerns were raised about these characterizations.

result: Critically, spatially specific neural suppression in EVC was observed even during omission trials when search displays were anticipated but not presented, with BOLD responses at HPDL and NL-near locations suppressed compared to NL-far. This demonstrates that suppression emerges proactively, activated merely by cues predicting search onset, supporting the proactive deployment of spatial priority maps.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly highlighted the omission trial findings as a key contribution. Reviewer 1 stated suppression 'also occurs in advance of any item actually appearing.' Reviewer 2 noted suppression 'was even present in trials in which the search display was omitted.' Reviewer 3 emphasized the study 'speaks to open questions about whether such suppression/enhancement is observed only in response to the arrival of visual information, or instead is preparatory, favouring the latter view.' The proactive interpretation was universally accepted without challenge.

result: Post-experiment questionnaire data showed only 35.7% of participants correctly identified the HPDL (not significantly different from 25% chance), and control analyses excluding aware participants yielded identical results, demonstrating that the observed neural suppression reflects implicit rather than explicit learning strategies.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically praised the 'careful application of follow-up analyses to rule out alternative, strategy-based accounts of the findings,' directly endorsing the implicit learning interpretation. Reviewers 1 and 2 raised no concerns about the implicit nature of learning or the control analyses. The evidence ruling out explicit strategies was accepted without question.

result: Despite neural suppression at HPDL and NL-near locations, behavioral data showed no costs for target identification at these locations, with Bayesian tests providing evidence for the absence of RT and accuracy differences across target locations, ruling out the alternative explanation that increased attention to NL-far drives the neural pattern.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly noted the study included 'careful application of follow-up analyses to rule out alternative, strategy-based accounts,' which encompasses these control analyses. No reviewer questioned the behavioral target data or the interpretation that neural suppression does not impair target processing. The dissociation between neural suppression and behavioral performance was implicitly accepted.

result: Control analyses demonstrated that results were qualitatively similar across different ROI mask sizes (small to medium) and with or without normalization, confirming the robustness and reliability of the main findings independent of specific analysis parameters.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically praised 'tests of the robustness of the findings to detailed analysis parameters such as ROI size' and 'exclusion of the role of regional baseline differences in BOLD responses,' directly endorsing these control analyses. No concerns were raised about methodological robustness by any reviewer.

result: The combined findings demonstrate that the brain leverages implicitly learned prior knowledge to optimize sensory processing through spatially broad, proactive, stimulus-unspecific suppression in EVC, which is then refined by downstream processing stages to produce spatially specific behavioral effects, fitting within the framework of spatial priority maps and highlighting a multifaceted distractor suppression process.
evaluation: All reviewers endorsed the overall interpretation and theoretical framework. Reviewer 1 stated the work 'will be of great interest to psychologists and neuroscientists examining attention, perception, learning and prediction.' Reviewer 2 called it 'a beautiful addition to the literature.' Reviewer 3 noted the study 'provides an advance over previous studies' and addresses 'theoretical debates in this literature on how distractor suppression unfolds.' The integration of findings into spatial priority map frameworks was accepted without challenge.

result: Distractors evoked larger BOLD responses than neutral stimuli, likely reflecting a combination of top-down modulation due to target relevance and bottom-up effects of distractor salience.
evaluation: No reviewer questioned these basic stimulus-evoked response differences or their interpretation. The findings are consistent with established attention literature and were implicitly accepted as part of the overall pattern of results.

result: Exploratory analyses suggested that distractor suppression patterns may differ between V1 and V2, with V2 mirroring the combined EVC results while V1 showed only partial modulation that was less robust and spatially broad, though these findings are tentative due to methodological limitations.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly noted that 'the main findings are enhanced by supplementary analyses that distinguish between the responses of early visual areas,' directly endorsing the V1/V2 exploratory analyses. No concerns were raised about these supplementary findings, though their exploratory and tentative nature was acknowledged by the authors.
